learningObjective: Diagnose the performance impact of register spilling on GPU kernels and identify why 'local memory' spills traverse HBM.

canonicalClaims.claim: On NVIDIA GPUs, per-thread 'local memory' is physically stored in global memory (HBM), with caching in L1/L2. Register spills therefore incur potentially hundreds of cycles of latency and consume HBM bandwidth when the caches don't absorb the traffic.
conditions: Kernel exceeds the register budget selected by the compiler (via --maxrregcount, __launch_bounds__, or heuristics).
Spill accesses are not fully absorbed by L1/L2.
nonImplications: Does not imply every spill costs full HBM latency; L1/L2 hits are common for repeated slot access.
Does not imply lower --maxrregcount is always better; forced spills often outweigh occupancy gains.

misconceptions.claim: Spills go to shared memory automatically.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Shared memory is programmer-managed and per-block; the compiler does not implicitly redirect register spills there.

misconceptions.claim: There is a dedicated on-chip spill buffer separate from HBM.
misconceptions.whyWrong: No such tier exists; spills back to local memory (backed by HBM) via L1/L2.

misconceptions.claim: Register spills are always free because L1 always hits.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Cache hit rate for spills depends on access frequency, working set size, and L1 pressure from other data. Cold spills reach HBM.

implementationFacts: ptxas info line reports 'spill stores' and 'spill loads' in bytes per thread.
Local memory is per-thread, logically private, but backed by global memory physically.
performanceScenarios: Attention kernels with large register footprints can experience heavy spill traffic; hand-tuned kernels (FlashAttention) restructure register usage to avoid this.
